## {auto-animate=true}

:::: {.repeat-row}
```{r}
#| output: asis
show_pair(
  list("unbiased", zoom = TRUE, avg = 6),
  list("biased", rows = 5, avg = 6)
)
```

<!-- Click 4 (Matt, 2026-10-18): names the imagined runs as the
frequentist idea, once, on its own click; gone at the next click (the
biased column), so the later clicks move up one (biased 5, averages 6,
definition 7). The Bayesian contrast comes at the start of Section 4.
r-stack: the definition sits where it does on slides 7-9. -->

::: {.repeat-def .r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4}
Frequentists imagine many runs so we can judge how sure we can be
:::
::: {.fragment fragment-index=7}
**Bias** is where the answers are centred, relative to the true answer
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
One study gives one answer and one plate. This is our experiment: the
brick is our best guess, and the plate shows how far off that guess could
be. The plate is the middle of a bell around the guess: the wider the
bell, the less sure we can be. We only ever have this one row. We built
the data, so we know the true answer.

The plate is a claim about something we never see: if we ran the same
study again and again, the answers would land about this far apart. Bias,
variance and coverage are all about those imagined runs. We'll leave the
plates aside for now and come back to them.

These imagined runs are how the frequentist approach (the usual one)
judges how sure we can be: its plate is a promise about them. We can also
use them to check any method, including the Bayesian one at the end.

Unbiased: the answers are centred on the true answer. Biased: the same
scatter, centred off to one side. Running the study more often doesn't
help; the average stays in the wrong place.
:::

<!-- Low vs high variance: the same bricks, the right column 2.5 times as
spread (same order, our experiment in the same row, now well away from
the line). Click 1 a bell over each column (how the answers spread) with
its spread bracket (the bell's middle), click 2 the definition. -->

## {auto-animate=true}

:::: {.repeat-row}
```{r}
#| output: asis
show_pair(
  list("low", bracket = 1),
  list("high", bracket = 1)
)
```

::: {.fragment .repeat-def fragment-index=2}
**Variance** is how spread out the answers are across repeated runs
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Both columns are centred on the true answer. The only difference is how
spread out the answers are. The bell shows how the answers would pile up
over many runs; the bracket measures the middle of it.

Our experiment is the same run in both columns. With low variance it lands
near the true answer; with high variance the same run lands well away.
This is the variance of the answer from run to run, not the variance in
the data.
:::

<!-- Honest vs overconfident plates: identical bricks, the bells and
brackets kept from the variance slide. Click 1 one plate per brick, row by
row (honest = as long as the bracket; overconfident = much shorter); click
2 our brick's own bell (grey, the plate's bell, as on the zoom) beside the
column's: as wide when honest, much narrower when overconfident; click 3
the plates that miss turn red (4 of 7, both sides, our experiment among
them); click 4 the definition. -->

## {auto-animate=true}

:::: {.repeat-row}
```{r}
#| output: asis
show_pair(
  list("honest", bracket = 0, plates = 1, ownbell = 2, miss = 3),
  list("over", bracket = 0, plates = 1, ownbell = 2, miss = 3)
)
```

::: {.fragment .repeat-def fragment-index=4}
**Coverage** is how often each run's plate reaches the true answer, compared with how often it promises to (often set at 95%)
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**Same answers in both columns: honest plates are as long as the real
spread, so they reach the true answer as often as they promise;
overconfident plates are too short, so they miss more often.**

Same bricks in both columns; only the plates differ. In a real study we
see one row, and its plate comes from the standard error: that run's own
guess at how spread out the bricks would be across all runs. The grey
bell is our brick's own bell, the one its plate comes from. Honest: it is
as wide as the real spread of the bricks, so the plate is as long as the
bracket. Overconfident: it is much narrower than the real spread, so the
plates are short and many miss.

A 95% plate promises to reach the true answer in about 95 of every 100
runs. That is a promise about the procedure (same design, same model, new
data each time), not about our one plate. Honest doesn't mean always
right: with many more runs, about 1 in 20 honest plates would miss too.
With only 7 runs drawn here, none of them do.

Coverage can't be checked in a real study; only a simulation with a known
true answer can check it. It fails when the plate is shorter than the real
spread (for example counting 120 builds as if they were 120 separate
sessions), or when the answers are biased (next slide). The other
direction (plates too long: less sure than we need to be) is also a
coverage problem.
:::

<!-- Bias breaks coverage too: both columns have honest plates (as long as
the bracket); the right column's bricks are shifted as on the bias slide,
its bracket centred on its average. Click 1 the misses turn red (4 of 7,
all on the far side), click 2 the line. -->

## {auto-animate=true}

:::: {.repeat-row}
```{r}
#| output: asis
show_pair(
  list("unbiased_honest", bracket = 0, plates = 0, miss = 1),
  list("biased_honest", bracket = 0, plates = 0, miss = 1)
)
```

::: {.fragment .repeat-def fragment-index=2}
Honest plates still miss when the answers are centred in the wrong place
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Both columns have honest plates, as long as the spread. But the biased
answers are centred to one side, so the plates miss on that side, more
often than they promise. Bias breaks coverage too.
:::

## {.center}

<!-- Summary of the three problems (Matt, 2026-10-17): the biased, high
variance and overconfident columns side by side, one line each, one per
click (brick_dag.R show_column). Lines Matt's (bias / vary / cover), also
under the towers on the next slide; all three goals since 2026-10-19 late
(Matt). -->

:::: {.repeat-row .repeat-summary}
::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| output: asis
show_column("biased", avg = 0)
```

Answers **centre** on the truth
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| output: asis
show_column("high", bracket = 0)
```

Answers **vary** no more <br> than they need to
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| output: asis
show_column("over", bracket = 0, plates = 0, ownbell = 0, miss = 0)
```

Plates **cover** the truth <br> as often as they claim
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Three ways to go wrong. Bias: the answers land to one side. Variance: the
answers spread more than they need to. Coverage: each plate should be as
long as the spread; here they are shorter, so they claim more certainty
than the spread allows.
:::


## Adding pieces

<!-- One tower per problem (Matt, 2026-10-09): a grey base brick with the
technical name, the section bricks that fix it stacked on top in talk
order (brick_dag.R show_fixes). Opens on the three bases; one click per
section adds that section's brick to every tower it fixes: Building the
model (Bias, Coverage), Multilevel (Coverage; off Variance since
2026-10-19, Matt: partial pooling's trade is for one session's level, not
the instruction answer, so its columns slide was cut), GLM (Bias; off
Coverage since 2026-10-18, Matt: its coverage picture was cut), Bayesian
(Variance since 2026-10-19, Matt: the sensible-prior slide, 38; Coverage).
Coverage ends tallest: it is the talk's main thread. Title is a
placeholder (Matt rewords). -->

```{r}
#| output: asis
show_fixes(shown = 1, frag = 2:5)
```

::: {.notes}
Each tower is one of the problems we just saw.

We are building up the pieces here: each section adds a brick to the
towers it helps, the way LEGO bricks lock together, overlapping the brick
below. The sideways overlap is just how bricks stack; it doesn't mean
"off to one side" the way the shifted bricks did on the bias slides.
(Neil read the offset as bias; Matt kept the offset and says this aloud,
2026-10-17.)

Building the model: choosing which pieces go in, and which stay out,
keeps the answers centred on the true answer; counting the evidence the
right way makes the plates long enough.

Multilevel structure: when the data come in groups, the model counts the
evidence by group itself, without us doing it by hand.

GLM: a model that matches the kind of outcome we have, so the answers
aren't pulled to one side.

Priors: writing down what we already know keeps the answers from varying
more than they need to, and keeps the plates honest when data are thin.

Coverage is the tallest tower: most of today is about how sure we can be.
:::

:::

Here, we want more sessions, not just more builds
:::

::: {.notes}
Format was decided once per session, so sessions are the evidence. More
people sharpen each session's average, but sessions still differ for
reasons we never measured, and more people can't remove that. Past a
point, only more sessions make us more sure about the instruction
format: ten times the people barely helps; twice the sessions helps a
lot. Plan this before collecting data.
:::

## The same people, building twice

<!-- Sequence A is explained on this DAG alone (Matt, 2026-10-09); the data
figure (lego_figs.R seq_a_plots) is no longer shown, and this slide took
its title. Session factors point into both builds, so comparing a
session's build 1 with its own build 2 cancels what the session shares; the
same people build twice, so their traits cancel too. The only slide with
Learning and Participant traits (Matt, 2026-10-08), so it uses the "full"
layout (bottom row). Clicks (Matt, 2026-10-09): the split into build 1 /
build 2 (4), then Learning (14), then Participant traits (13). Captions


::: {.r-stack}
::: {.dag-note .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}
Everyone builds twice, so errors split into build 1 and build 2
:::
::: {.dag-note .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2}
Time matters: people learn between builds
:::
::: {.dag-note .fragment fragment-index=3}
People differ too, in ways we never measure
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Within a session the same people build twice, so their differences cancel
too. Don't say the comparison is helped by sessions alone.

Accuracy line (HANDOFF_brick_dag_2026-10-19_evening.md §5): the full model for these data also needs a term
for each person, because everyone built twice. We keep the story on

be. Comparing each person with themselves gives a short plate that still
reaches it.

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Adding errors on the first build means comparing builders who made the
same number of errors the first time.

Two builders each made, say, 8 errors on build 1. One had picture
instructions: about what picture instructions produce, so nothing unusual
about their session. The other had text instructions, which should have
given fewer. To make 8 anyway, their session was probably worse: a noisier
room, a less clear experimenter.

So once we hold build-1 errors fixed, text instructions go with worse
sessions. Nothing causes that link; it's what we can work out about the
session. Worse sessions add errors on build 2 too, which hides part of the
real benefit of text.

The same happens through people's own traits, which this picture leaves
out.

The red arc is the answer being damaged, not part of the path. The path
is Instructions → Build 1 ← Session → Build 2.
:::

## When format is given by session, the session is the unit

<!-- Before the random-effect DAG (Matt, 2026-10-20; replaces the 19 Oct
"what a random effect allows for, and what it assumes" explainer: the
confounding half and the dice are cut). brick_dag.R show_rooms, drawn by
hand in the next-but-one slide's look. Opens on the left half, format
given to each person: builds scattered, the format averages and the gap;
click 1 caption, people; click 2 the right half, format given to each
session: the same gap, builds in yellow session bands; click 3 caption,
sessions; click 4 the rule, which stays (Matt's "test the effect against
the variation among the units it was assigned to", made plainer; given to
people, the yardstick is how much people differ, not build-level noise:
that needs each person to build with both formats). "More people per
session barely helps" is now in the notes; slide 16's "Here, we want more
sessions, not just more builds" says it on screen (Matt: keep both). Title
and captions placeholders; Matt rewords. -->

```{r}
#| output: asis
show_rooms(frag = 2)
```

::: {.r-stack}
::: {.dag-note .long .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}
If each person got their own format, <br> the difference would have to stand out from how much people differ
:::

::: {.dag-note .long .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3}
In our study, each session got a format, <br> so the difference must stand out from how much sessions differ
:::

::: {.dag-note .long .fragment fragment-index=4}
Whatever gets the format, people or sessions, <br> the difference must stand out from how much they differ
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**Judge a difference against how much the things that got the format
differ. Our sessions got the format, so the difference must stand out from
how much sessions differ. If each person had got their own format, it
would only have to stand out from how much people differ.**

Left: format given to each person. Each small model is one person's build;
the dashed lines are the formats' averages, the bar between them the gap.
People differ a lot, but with many people their differences average out of
each format's average.

Right: the same gap, but the builds come in sessions (yellow). Builds in a
session share a room and an experimenter, so they run high or low together,
and every build in a session had the same format. So each format's average
rests on three sessions, not thirty people.

So more people per session barely helps: they make each session's average
sharper, but they can't change how much sessions differ. Only more
sessions average those differences out. The next slide adds the piece that
lets the model see this: a random effect, which learns how much sessions
differ.

If asked, what if each person built once with each format? Then each
person is compared with themselves, and the difference only has to stand
out from how much one person's builds vary, as with learning on slide 17.
Giving formats to people within sessions does something similar for
sessions: every session has both formats, so how much sessions differ
cancels out.

The picture spreads the sessions further apart than our study does: there,
sessions differ about as much as builds within a session do.

If asked, how much does each help? In our design, twice the people per
session makes the format answer's plate a few percent shorter; twice the
sessions, about 30% shorter. The more sessions differ compared with people,
the sooner more people stop helping.

If asked, why not put session in as an ordinary factor? Every session has
one format, so the session terms soak up the format. R returns NA for
format, or, if format is listed first, a "format" number that is really
one session compared with another.
:::

Transformed vs count model (Matt, 2026-10-19; Option E in the vault note

click 3 the count model's line (orange); the yellow line stays. Slide 31

2026-10-19). Untitled, as the other figure slides. "Yellow" above is
light orange since 2026-10-19 late (Matt: yellow is the random effect's
colour; pal$orange light). -->

```{r}
#| output: asis
show_counts()
```

::: {.r-stack}
::: {.dag-note .fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
Many builds have no errors; some have one or two
:::
<!-- ::: {.dag-note .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}
A [normal model]{.bell-word} expects some builds to have fewer than no errors
:::
::: {.dag-note .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2}
Usually we'd [transform]{.bell-word} the errors to fit the long tail
:::
::: {.dag-note .fragment fragment-index=3}
A [count model]{.count-word} fits the counts as they are
::: -->
:::

::: {.notes}
**With counts like these, a normal model expects builds with fewer than no
errors, a transformed model fixes that but comes back too low, and a count
model fits the counts as they are.**

A general case, not our study: a build where many people make no errors
and some make one or two. Each brick is one build, stacked over how many
errors it had. A few builds have more. Skewed, with a long tail.

A normal model on the errors as they are, with the same average and
spread, is symmetric, so it spills past "no errors": it expects some
builds to have fewer than no errors, which can't happen (the red part).
It also misses the pile at no errors and the long tail on the right.

The usual fix is to transform the errors first, for example taking logs
(of errors plus one, so no errors still works), fitting a normal model to
that, then converting the answer back to errors. The light orange line is that
transformed model, shown back on the error scale. No more impossible
values, but squeezing the tail gives the few builds with many errors less
weight, so it piles up at the low end. Converted back, its answer
describes a typical build, which is lower than the average build.

The count model describes the counts as they are: whole numbers from no
errors upwards, with a long tail. The orange line. (It is a negative
binomial: these counts vary more than the simplest count model, the
Poisson, expects.)

The picture exaggerates the gap to make it visible; next we'll see what it
does to our answer, run after run. (Our main study's error counts are
high, so there the plain normal model does fine; the trouble starts when
counts are low.)
:::

##

<!-- The count model's Bias fix (the piece, how it works, then what it
fixes). Option E (Matt, 2026-10-19; vault note "2026-10-19 Count model
return - what it fixes"): the format answer, transformed model vs count
model. Columns of repeats (brick_dag.R show_pair, "glm_trans" /
"glm_count"), the general case placed by hand: the transformed model
centres one run-to-run spread low (the desktop chat's 300 repeats: 0.36
to 0.9 spreads), the count model on the true answer. One change: the
centre. Click 1 the averages and the Bias line (a placeholder; Matt
rewords). Headings in the lines' colours, as on slide 29. Never claim the
transform makes the format difference look smaller: with session effects
it doesn't. No Coverage picture: GLM is on the Bias tower only (slide

:::: {.repeat-row .repeat-wide}
```{r}
#| output: asis
show_pair(
    list("glm_trans", avg = 1),
    list("glm_count", avg = 1),
    tie = FALSE
)
```

::: {.repeat-def}
Errors per format?

<br>

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
**Bias:** the [transformed model's]{.bell-word} answers centre too low
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**Run after run, the transformed model's answers centre too low, while the
count model's centre on the true answer.**

Back to our question: how many errors does each format give? Imagine
running the study many times and fitting both models each time.

The transformed model works on the log scale. Averaging there and
converting back gives a typical build, not the average build: squeezing
the long tail gives the few builds with many errors less weight, so the
answer comes back too low, run after run. That is bias.

The count model works with the errors as they are, so its answers centre
on the true answer. One catch: in a model with sessions and people, the
answer has to be averaged over sessions and people too. The quick
version, the answer for a typical session, also comes back a little low
(in brms, posterior_epred with re_formula = NA gives the quick version).

How low? In a check of 300 repeats of our design, about a third to a
whole run's spread, depending on how the errors arise. The picture shows
the general case.

The comparison between formats as a ratio (how many times as many errors
text gives as pictures) is fine under every model at our study's error
counts; it is each format's own answer that
the transform pulls down. A plain normal model on the raw errors would
also centre on the true average; its problem was the shape, not the
average.
:::

::: {.dag-note}
Pick the model whose shape matches your outcome
:::

::: {.notes}
Counts are one case. The same idea works for any outcome: choose the
model whose shape matches what the outcome can and can't do.

Time to finish: never less than no time, and a few builds take much
longer. A gamma model, for example.

Share of bricks correct: between none and all, and most builds are close
to all. A beta model, for example.

Number of errors, picture vs text: the shape itself can depend on a predictor. Here
text instructions give fewer errors and more consistent builds: a
narrower curve. A distributional model lets the spread, not just the
average, differ by format. (Strictly this goes beyond GLMs; in brms it is
one extra line for the spread.)

The normal and count models, and the gamma model for time, are
generalised linear models (GLMs). More in a future workshop.
:::

## Do text instructions lead to fewer errors?

<!-- Revised 2026-10-19 (Matt's brief): the way people intuitively read a
frequentist result is the Bayesian reading. Lay audience: no numbers, no
new concepts. Opens Section 4, before the prior goes on the DAG
(brick_dag.R show_answers). Two columns with the same brick on the same
plate. Click 1 the imagined runs (frequentist); 2 the bell after the
data (Bayesian); 3 the dashed "no difference" lines, crossing the plate
as in our study, and the bell's text side shaded; 4 the shared sentence
"Text probably leads to fewer errors." (italic, below the plots); 5 red cross, "Tempting, but not allowed." + why; 6 green tick, "Allowed." + why. (The
punchline "Most people already read results the Bayesian way." was
removed completely, Matt, 2026-10-19.) The green
prior curve, "prior", "<- text: fewer errors" and all earlier captions
were removed, so "prior" first appears on slide 36 (the notes here still
introduce it aloud). "posterior" and "credible interval" in the notes
only. The summary slide's middle panel calls back to this slide. -->

```{r}
#| output: asis
show_answers()
```

::: {.notes}
**Same plate, two readings: "text probably leads to fewer errors" is
tempting but not allowed from the frequentist plate, and exactly what the
Bayesian answer allows.**

First, what Bayesian gives us; then back to that question.

Same data, same plate, two ways of reading it. Same length here to keep
the comparison simple; with few sessions the Bayesian plate comes out
longer (slide 38).

Frequentist, the usual approach and what we've used so far: the plate is
a promise about the method. Run the study again and again (the faint
plates), and plates made this way reach the true answer most of the time.

Bayesian: start from what we believed before seeing the data (a prior;
the next slide puts one on the model), then let the data update it. What
comes out is this hill: where the true answer probably is, given the data
(technically the posterior; the plate under it is a credible interval).

Our plate crosses "no difference", as it did with our 6 sessions, but
most of it, and most of the hill, sits on the text side.

So the sentence everyone wants to write: text probably leads to fewer
errors.

From the frequentist plate, that sentence is tempting but not allowed:
the method catches the truth most of the time, but it says nothing about
how likely this particular plate is to hold it, or how likely it is that
text helps. (If asked: "not significant" fairly means we couldn't rule
out no difference; it still can't say how likely it is that text helps.)

From the Bayesian hill, it is exactly what the hill answers: most of it
is on the text side, so text probably helps, though we can't be sure.

The two plates are different objects, but we can still check either one
against the imagined runs: how often does it reach the true answer? That
is how this section ends.
:::

## A prior on how much sessions differ

<!-- Section 4's DAG step (+11), after the contrast: the green prior plate
stacks on Session factors (the baseplate grows to hold it; on the
Normal/Gaussian plate until that was dropped, 2026-10-18). Title a
placeholder. -->

```{r}
#| output: asis
show_dag(upto = 10, frag = 11)
```

::: {.dag-note .fragment fragment-index=1}
How much sessions differ gets a prior, <br> so our uncertainty about it carries through to every answer
:::

::: {.notes}
In a Bayesian model every piece gets a prior. The one on the diagram is
the prior on how much sessions differ; we meet a second one later in this
section.

Strictly, what carries the uncertainty through is the Bayesian fit itself:
it keeps every amount of difference that fits the data and averages the
answer over them. The prior is what makes that possible, and it keeps how
much sessions differ from being pinned at exactly zero.
:::

## One guess at how much sessions differ, or every amount that fits

<!-- How the prior works (Matt, 2026-10-19; IDEAS section 3 visual 1), the
general case drawn by hand (brick_dag.R show_spread): how much sessions
differ along one baseline, "sessions alike" to "differ a lot", no
numbers. Click 1 the usual fit's one guess (a yellow brick: session level
is yellow); click 2 the prior (green: highest at "alike", falling
gently, the half-normal shape used in practice; Matt, 2026-10-19); click
3 the curve after the data (yellow): still wide with 6 sessions, peaking
over the brick. Captions one at a time in one spot, the last stays.
Title and captions placeholders (Matt rewords). -->

```{r}
#| output: asis
show_spread()
```

::: {.r-stack}
::: {.dag-note .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}
A frequentist fit makes one guess
:::

::: {.dag-note .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2}
The prior, what we expect before the data: <br> modest differences likely, big ones allowed
:::

::: {.dag-note .fragment fragment-index=3}
With 6 sessions, many amounts of difference still fit the data
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
How much do sessions differ? That number sets how sure we can be about
the format answer, so it matters.

The frequentist fit makes one guess, the single most likely value, and then
carries on as if it were exactly right.

The Bayesian model starts from a prior: modest differences are likely,
big ones are allowed. This is the kind of prior people actually use, not
"anything goes".

After the data, many amounts of difference still fit: with only 6
sessions, the data can't pin it down. The Bayesian model keeps all of
them, weighted by how well they fit, instead of betting on one.

Backstage, not to say as a number: in our simulated study the one guess
was well below how much sessions really differ, and the data fit anything from no
difference at all upwards.
:::

##

<!-- The prior's Coverage fix (Matt, 2026-10-19; the piece, how it works,
then what it fixes): slide 8's honest / overconfident columns, lean (no
bells or brackets), for the format answer, the general case for a count
model with few sessions (brick_dag.R show_pair, "bayes_known" /
"bayes_prior"; drawn by hand, not simulated). Same bricks; one change:
the plate. Headings in the colours of the last slide's pieces (yellow
brick, green prior). Click 1 the plates, click 2 the misses turn red
(rows 1 and 7 of "One guess"; our experiment reaches the line, as on
slide 26), click 3 the Coverage line (wording a placeholder). Nothing
here claims Bias or Variance: the Bayesian brick's place on slide 11's
Variance tower comes from the next slide. -->

:::: {.repeat-row}
```{r}
#| output: asis
show_pair(
    list("bayes_known", plates = 1, miss = 2),
    list("bayes_prior", plates = 1, miss = 2),
    tie = FALSE
)
```

::: {.repeat-def}
Instruction format

<br>

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
**Coverage:** the plates are too short and miss more often than they promise; <br> with a prior, they reach the true answer about as often as they claim
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Back to our question, the instruction format, now with the count model.
Imagine running the study many times. Same answers in both columns; only
the plates differ.

With one guess of how much sessions differ, treated as known, the plates come out a
little too short, so they miss more often than the promised 1 in 20. The
picture exaggerates how short they are. This is what the usual
count-model software gives by default. (Profile or
bootstrap plates partly allow for the uncertainty; for the normal model,
small-sample corrections do the job without a prior.)

With a prior on how much sessions differ, that uncertainty carries into
the format answer: the plates are longer, and they
reach the true answer about as often as they claim. That is the usual
pattern with few groups and a sensible prior; we haven't simulated it
here.

Our own experiment reached the true answer either way, as on the
multilevel slide. Coverage is about the procedure across runs, not one
plate.
:::

##

<!-- The Bayesian piece's Variance fix (Matt, 2026-10-19, from the vault
handoff "Sensible prior bias-variance trade-off"; Matt chose: after the
Coverage return, the prior in the bell strip, "Almost no prior" drawn very
wide, Bayesian added to slide 11's Variance tower). The layout of the cut
partial-pooling columns slide (Matt, 2026-10-19), but for the format
answer ("Instruction format" above the columns); since the cut, the first
three-column comparison, so the notes set it up. A different prior from slide 35's:
a prior on the format answer, not on the spread. The general case with
thin data, drawn by hand (positions and the check in brick_dag.R,
"fx_none" / "fx_sensible" / "fx_strong"). One change between columns: how
strong the prior is (green, centred on the dashed "no difference" line).
Opens on "Almost no prior" with its prior; click 1 the sensible prior and
its column, row by row; click 2 the brackets; click 3 average markers;
click 4 "Very strong prior"; click 5 the closing line. Captions follow
the cut partial-pooling slide's (placeholders; Matt rewords). -->

::: {.dag-note}
Instruction format
:::

:::: {.repeat-row .repeat-trio .repeat-labelled}
```{r}
#| output: asis
show_trio(
    list("fx_none", prior = 0, bracket = 2, bell = FALSE, avg = 3),
    list(
        "fx_sensible",
        rows = 1,
        prior = 1,
        bracket = 2,
        bell = FALSE,
        avg = 3
    ),
    list("fx_strong", rows = 4, prior = 4, avg = 4, avg_low = TRUE)
)
```
::::

::: {.r-stack}
::: {.dag-note .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2}
Less **variance**: the answers spread much less
:::
::: {.dag-note .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3}
A little **bias**: they are pulled toward "no difference"
:::
::: {.dag-note .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=4}
Pulled all the way: no spread, but well off-centre
:::
::: {.dag-note .fragment fragment-index=5}
Overall, the answers with a sensible prior sit closest to the true answer
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**A sensible prior pulls the answers a little toward "no difference" but
makes them vary much less, so overall they land closest to the true
answer.**

Imagine running the study many times and working out the instruction
answer each time, one brick per run, as on the variance slides at the
start. The only change between the columns is how strong a prior we put
on that answer. This is a different prior from the one on how much sessions differ: a
prior on the format answer itself, centred on "no difference".

Almost no prior: the answers are centred on the true answer but spread
widely. A sensible prior says big effects are unlikely, not that there is
no effect: the answers are pulled a little toward "no difference" and
spread much less. A very strong prior at "no difference" swamps the data:
every answer lands on "no difference", no spread, always off by the same
amount.

Being a little off-centre is worth it when the answers become much less
spread out, so the middle column sits closest to the true answer overall.

Why pull toward "no difference"? It is the cautious direction: the prior
makes us a little slower to claim an effect, not quicker.

Unlike the collider (slide 20), which also pulled the answers toward "no
difference": this pull is stated openly in the prior, it is small, and it
fades as the data grow. The collider's pull was hidden, and it made the
plates too short as well.

This is the general case, when data are thin (here, few sessions per
format), not a claim about our study's data. With plenty of data the
prior's pull fades, and the first two columns look alike. A
sensible prior helps when the true effect is the size we expected; if the
true effect were huge, a prior that called it unlikely would cost more
than it saves.
:::

## Frequentist fits work for many designs

<!-- The section's summary (Matt, 2026-10-19, grilled first; was "Bayesian
is a piece too"): sell switching to Bayesian as a whole approach, not just
a prior on the spread. Opening line on from the start; three small panels
(brick_dag.R show_benefits), one per click, each calling back to its
full-size picture (38, 35, 37); the line under each carries any condition
(honest plates matter when data are thin). Click 4 keeps the old slide's
limit. "It earns it with few groups, small samples, or a model that won't
run" went: panel 1 says it. Left out on purpose: "it may decide sessions
don't differ at all" (rare at the simulated spread; cut before) and any
claim that frequentist fits can't give honest plates (small-sample
corrections exist for the linear model). -->

<br>

```{r}
#| output: asis
show_benefits()
```

<br>

::: {.dag-note .fragment fragment-index=4}
It can't rescue a model built from the wrong pieces.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Frequentist fits work for many designs; Bayesian adds three things:
honest plates, particularly when data are thin; a statement of where the
true answer probably is; and an open way to use what we already know.**

For many designs, with plenty of data at every level, the usual
frequentist fit and a Bayesian fit give similar answers. For simple linear
models there are also small-sample corrections. So this isn't "frequentist
is wrong". It's what you gain by switching.

Honest plates, particularly when data are thin: with few groups, small samples or
a complex model, the frequentist fit treats its guess at things like how much
sessions differ as known, so its plates come out too short. The
Bayesian fit keeps every value that fits the data, so its plates are as
long as they should be, and reach the true answer about as often as they
claim. (Slide 38.)

Says where the true answer probably is: a Bayesian plate is a statement
about this study: the true difference probably lies in here. It can also
say directly how likely it is that text instructions lead to fewer errors:
the shaded part of the bell. That's the question people actually ask; a
frequentist plate is a promise about many imagined runs. (Slide 35.)

If asked "doesn't a bootstrapped interval do this?": the bootstrap
re-draws our own data to imagine the re-runs, so its plate makes the same
promise as any frequentist plate. Its hill is answers across re-runs, not
where the true answer probably is: "93% of re-run answers favour text" is
not "a 93% chance text helps". With plenty of data the numbers are often
close to a Bayesian answer with a vague prior; the difference is what
you're allowed to say. (The Bayesian bootstrap does allow the "probably"
reading, because it is a Bayesian method.) In our study the bootstrap is
also thin: re-drawing builds is the 120-builds mistake; re-drawing 3
sessions per format gives only 10 combinations per format and plates
about a fifth too short.

Uses what we already know, openly: we know sessions of people building
LEGO won't differ by enormous amounts, and error counts sit in a
believable range. The prior writes that down where everyone can see it.
(Slide 37.)

If asked "isn't that subjective?": the prior is stated and can be checked.
If a reasonable change to the prior changes the answer, that tells you the
data are thin.

Last click: it can't rescue a model built from the wrong pieces, like the
collider or ignoring the sessions.
:::

much sessions differ. Left out on purpose: errors on the first build
(slide 20).

The diagram shows the prior on how much sessions differ; the prior on the
format answer (slide 39) isn't drawn.

## Every piece earns its place

<!-- Recap as the towers again (Matt, 2026-10-19; replaces the five-line
list, which predated Option E, slide 38 and slide 39): slide 11's picture
rebuilt, same show_fixes() call, one click per section adding its bricks
to every tower it fixes; the caption under the towers says how that
section earned each brick (tower word bold), fading at the next click; the
last stays. Each line claims only what its section showed: Coverage for
the multilevel model is "counts sessions itself", not "as sure as the
design allows" (slide 38: still a little short with 6 sessions); the count
model's Bias fix is against the transform (slide 31), not "no impossible
predictions" (the transform has none either); the collider line is about
the answers across runs, not our one answer (ours landed closer). Captions
are placeholders (Matt rewords). .recap in brick_dag.css is now unused.
Multilevel is off the Variance tower (Matt, 2026-10-19: partial pooling's
trade is for one session's level, not the instruction answer), so its
caption is the Coverage line only. -->

```{r}
#| output: asis
show_fixes(shown = 1, frag = 2:5, vb = "0 170 1200 410")
```

::: {.r-stack}
::: {.dag-note .long .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}
**Bias:** leave out errors on the first build <br>
**Coverage:** count the evidence as sessions, not builds
:::
::: {.dag-note .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=2}
**Coverage:** a random effect lets the model count sessions itself
:::
::: {.dag-note .fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=3}
**Bias:** a count model avoids systematically low answers
:::
::: {.dag-note .long .fragment fragment-index=4}
**Variance:** a sensible prior on the format answer <br>
**Coverage:** a prior on how much sessions differ
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The same towers as at the start, now with how each brick was earned.

Building the model: leaving errors on the first build out keeps the
answers centred on the true answer (slide 20); counting 6 sessions, not
120 builds, stops us being falsely sure (slide 15).

Multilevel: the random effect learns how much sessions differ, so the
model counts the evidence as sessions without us doing it by hand (slide
26). With 6 sessions its plates are still a little short; the prior
finishes that job.

Count model: each format's answer centres on the true answer; the
transformed model's comes back too low (slide 31).

Bayesian: a sensible prior on the format answer trades a little bias for
much less spread (slide 39); a prior on how much sessions differ carries
that uncertainty into the plates, so they reach the true answer about as
often as they claim (slide 38). And it lets us say what we wanted to say
all along: text probably leads to fewer errors (slide 35).

Coverage is the tallest tower: most of today was about how sure we can be.

Back to the subtitle: making variance work for you means building the
model so that how much the data vary (between sessions, in the counts)
sets how sure we can be.
:::
